author: fradamt
content: The exited validators don't contribute to p2p load. And if we end up *depending* on a smaller validator set in order to handle aggregation etc... we at least have the option of capping the set, which is much easier if it's smaller to begin with. E.g. much easier to be at 100k validators and set a 128k cap than to do that with 500k validators

author: ladidan
content:
I guess in aggregate the common patterns are:

- They provide non-custodial staking services, which means each client must send the request/tx from their own withdrawal address (often behind a custodian's wallet & approval flows)
- They put new stake on 0x02 but leave existing stake on 0x01 for a later phase. Migrating validators has been announced but not executed at scale
- Their withdrawal address is a smart contract, so the contract (and potentially governance) has to be upgraded before it can send consolidation requests
- They run custodial/pooled staking from a single withdrawal address, so it's basically up to internal decision-making; i.e. from the outside you can't see a technical blocker - it's likely about prioritisation/choice --> consolidations are an *optional* feature
- I've seen some mention entry/exit queue constraints (pausing of rewards)

author: wander1
content:
> I'd love to know more about these complexities. Where exactly is the technical debt (accounting, tooling, security, etc.)?

For NodeSet, we have an automated validator distribution system that allows 100+ vetted small operators to create validators to stake our customers' ETH with a smart contract as the designated withdrawal address. This system is was designed as a 5+ year investment and went live early last year before EIP-7251 was finalized, so it's only compatible with 0x01 validators. Staking does not generate sufficient profit for us to invest in updating this system yet, so if 0x02 validators are required, rather than unstake our customers' ~25k ETH, we would have to centralize this stake under a single operator.

We understand that Ethereum must evolve over time and that, to some extent, deprecation is necessary for this. However, it seems from my perspective that a hard 0x02 requirement impacts the long-tail of individuals more harshly than bigger operators. If it's a real issue for the protocol, I'd prefer to see some small (perhaps growing) incentive to switch. I.e. increase 0x02 validator rewards by some small amount. Because decentralized systems cost significantly more to develop and update than centralized ones, an opportunity cost like this is acceptable vs the cost to modify our system. Our customers are used to paying a small decentralization premium for safety, similar to staking insurance. On the other hand, all the big centralized stakers would be forced to change to remain competitive. 

Tl;dr: it's less disruptive to existing decentralized systems to create a careful deprecation schedule for 0x01 with corresponding incentives rather than a hard swap.
